children: By Gavin Bade in Washington and Santiago Pérez in Mexico City

The U.S. government is pressuring Mexican officials to accept new rules for exports of artificial-intelligence hardware to prevent Chinese companies and other foreign firms from circumventing tariffs, said people familiar with the negotiations.

The proposal would limit the amount of components that come from outside North America in the production of AI hardware, a set of products including chips and servers that has quickly become Mexico's top export to the U.S., surpassing automobiles this year.

Mexico and the U.S. are discussing the so-called rules of origin proposal as part of negotiations around revising the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trilateral free-trade deal that Trump has repeatedly threatened to abandon. While the U.S. has imposed tariffs on some Mexican goods, they largely remain much lower than levies on Chinese products.

A new round of talks between U.S. and Mexican trade officials is expected to take place in Washington as early as next week, said the people familiar with the negotiations. The two countries are also expected to discuss potential reductions to U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.

In addition to AI equipment, the U.S. could also propose rules to lower Chinese content and increase North American components for a litany of consumer products, such as medical equipment. While cars, auto parts and high-end computer chips are subject to tariffs from the Trump administration, more commonplace semiconductors used in the AI buildout can enter the U.S. largely tariff-free.

"China thinks that they can come in through the Western Hemisphere, bypass all our trade agreements and pretend that things are made in Mexico, but in reality they're Chinese products," said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R., Ohio), who has consulted with Mexican industry groups about the potential for rules of origin on new industries.
"We have to crack down on that, because what we don't want is a trade agreement that allows Mexico and Canada to be a gateway for China to circumvent trade restrictions," he added.

The White House, the Commerce Department and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative didn't respond to requests for comment. But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a July appearance at the Aspen Security Forum that he would push to expand rules of origin to other strategic sectors, like electronics and pharmaceuticals.
"The rules of origin for USMCA can be tightened on all these things," Greer said, adding that he was working with the Mexican government to identify which industries could be reshored.
Booming technology trade between Mexico and the U.S. is fueling America's red-hot AI buildup.

In the land port of Laredo, Texas, America's busiest trade gateway, computer imports stood at nearly $6 billion a year from 2021 through 2023. Then they jumped to $13.4 billion in 2024 and $30.8 billion in 2025, said Daniel Covarrubias, a trade expert at Texas A&M International University. In the first six months of this year, Mexico exported $83 billion of computer servers used in AI data centers-94% of it went to the U.S., an increase of more than 170%, according to S&P Global.
"The speed is the part that's hard to absorb," said Covarrubias, who leads the Texas Center for Border Economic and Enterprise Development

While overall U.S. imports from China declined amid steeper tariffs, Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn are using their vast presence across Mexico to manufacture AI servers and components for U.S. tech firms such as Nvidia. Such firms could be negatively affected by new rules of origin, depending on how many components they source from North America, versus importing from Asia.

Now, U.S. negotiators want AI equipment and other sectors to have the same sourcing rules already in place for the auto industry, where cars must have 75% or more of their content from North American suppliers to qualify for duty-free treatment.

The proposal remains in the early stages and the U.S. hasn't yet detailed how much content they would want to come from North America or the U.S. for each industry, and how much time they would give industries to adjust. The Trump administration could spell out its proposals further when the two sides meet again soon.

"Tech imports are increasing, and it's getting murky in terms of actual origin," said Jay Gerard, senior vice president at Worldwide Logistics Group, a U.S. freight forwarder and logistics firm. "Some type of scrutiny was expected."

Mexico has long seen China as a trade rival. Mexican officials have already agreed to impose higher duties on Chinese imports and take measures to prevent the transhipment of goods that are then exported to the U.S. tariff-free. But they want to prevent the imposition of specific rules demanding U.S. content that would in effect kill the North American free-trade deal.
Industry groups warn that adding sourcing rules to new industries would likely raise red tape and the cost of products.

The new U.S. demands on rules of origin could also complicate talks with Canada-if and when those negotiations can begin. Unlike Mexico, Canada and the U.S. haven't opened formal talks on USMCA yet, and instead are mired in an escalating tariff conflict.
